title: Personas
blurb: Explain what personas are for in the business case practice and how PRINCE2 Agile says they should be written: fictional, needs-based, co-written and few in number.
question: A marketing lead offers to write ten personas on her own, each based on the age and income of a real customer she knows. Which parts of this go against PRINCE2 Agile guidance on personas?

teach.body: Personas are fictional user profiles built around user needs. In PRINCE2 Agile they are a technique of the business case practice: they help identify and articulate the specific benefits that a proposed solution or project can deliver to its users, customers and stakeholders. By keeping a few vivid 'people' in view, the team keeps value and real user needs at the centre of decisions.

Historically, user groups were formed from demographic data. In agile the focus is on user needs, whether the users are external customers or internal or public users. Experience shows that age, occupation and income no longer predict who shares the same wants and needs, so a persona built on demographics is not helpful.

teach.h: Why fictional, why co-written, why few
teach.body: Fictional personas give a level of abstraction that leaves more room for innovation than a profile of one real person. Writing them in a cross-functional workshop with developers increases collaboration and helps the team identify with users. Keeping to five or fewer matters because too many user needs shift focus from key users, make prioritizing harder and take too long to meet deadlines.

teach.body: Greywater Leisure is building a booking app for its pools and gyms. In the project initiation workshop, the team coach brings together two developers, a tester, front-desk staff and the chief product owner. They write four fictional personas from user needs, such as 'Dev, who swims before a 7am shift and needs a lane guaranteed in under a minute'. None is a real member. The personas make the benefits concrete and help the product owners rank stories.

teach.text: Personas are a BUSINESS CASE technique (6.4.1), not a plans tool like the story map or an organization tool like the skill matrix. Do not build them on demographics or on a real person, and do not let one person write them alone. 'No more than five' applies to agile pilots and new products; at high agile maturity the set can be larger.

items: Personas help identify and articulate specific benefits for users, customers and stakeholders.
They are a technique of the business case practice (6.4.1).
Write them in a cross-functional workshop with development team members.
Keep them fictional: abstraction gives a broader range for innovation.
Base them on user needs, not demographics such as age, occupation or income.
No more than five for agile pilots or new products; more only at high agile maturity.

summary: You can now explain why personas are used in the business case practice and how PRINCE2 Agile says to write them. You can also spot a persona approach that breaks the guidance.

A.q: Why are personas valuable in business case development?
options: They set the team's decision-making authority
They help articulate the benefits a solution can deliver
They show the skills and gaps in each delivery team
They track the total risk exposure in each iteration
A.why: Personas help identify and articulate the specific benefits a proposed solution can deliver to users, customers and stakeholders (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Decision-making authority is agreed with delegation poker and recorded in a delegation matrix.
whyNot.2: Skills and gaps are shown on a team skill matrix.
whyNot.3: Total risk exposure is tracked with a cumulative risk burn-down chart.

A.q: On what should personas be based, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
A.why: In agile the focus is on user needs; demographics no longer represent people with the same wants and needs (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Demographics such as age, occupation and income are what the book says no longer predict shared needs.
whyNot.1: Personas represent users, not the board's views.
whyNot.3: Personas are fictional, not copies of real accounts.

A.q: How many personas does PRINCE2 Agile recommend as a maximum for an agile pilot project or a new product?
A.why: Anything above five is not recommended for agile pilots or new products; the set can be enlarged when agile maturity is high (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: One to three is the number of key user groups prioritized in the project canvas workshop, not the persona limit.
whyNot.2: Seven is above the recommended limit of five.
whyNot.3: Ten is well above the recommended limit of five.

B.q: Which practice are personas a technique of in PRINCE2 Agile?
B.why: Personas are described as valuable tools in business case development (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Organization techniques include the skill matrix and delegation poker.
whyNot.1: Plans techniques include story mapping and estimation; personas can feed a story map, but they belong to the business case.
whyNot.2: Quality techniques include the Definitions of Ready and Done and testing approaches.

B.q: Why does PRINCE2 Agile recommend that personas are fictional?
options: The level of abstraction leaves more room for innovation
Real customers cannot be named in project documents
Fictional personas can be written without user research
Fictional personas do not need reviewing later in the project
B.why: Personas should be fictional because the abstraction ensures a broader range for innovation (6.4.1).

whyNot.1: The book's reason is innovation, not a naming or legal rule.
whyNot.2: Personas still rest on real user needs; fiction is about abstraction, not skipping research.
whyNot.3: Personas guide product decisions and can be refined like other artifacts.

B.q: In which workshop is 'persona definition' an agenda topic?
B.why: The project initiation workshop includes 'persona definition': identify and define key user personas to guide product decisions (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: Kickoff covers team intro, psychological safety, values, skill and delegation matrices, and dashboards.
whyNot.2: The team retrospective covers the good, the bad, the learning and team building.
whyNot.3: Release planning covers introduction, OKR definition, release planning and wrap-up.

C.q:
Which two statements about writing personas are correct?
1. They should be written in a cross-functional workshop that includes development team members.
2. They should be based on a real customer known to the team.
3. They should be grouped by demographic data such as age and income.
4. A high level of agile maturity can justify a larger persona set.
C.why: Personas are best written in a cross-functional workshop with developers, and the set can be enlarged when agile maturity is high (6.4.1).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: personas should be fictional.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: personas are fictional and based on needs, not demographics.
whyNot.3: Statement 3 is wrong: demographics no longer represent shared wants and needs.

C.q: A user advocate offers to write the personas alone, basing each on someone she knows. What should the project manager recommend?
options: Let her write them, as she knows the users better than anyone
Co-write fictional personas in a cross-functional workshop
Ask the board to approve each persona before use
Base the personas on a customer survey of ages and incomes
C.why: Personas should be co-written in a cross-functional workshop with developers and kept fictional; the advocate should take part rather than write them alone (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Writing them alone, from real people, loses collaboration and abstraction.
whyNot.2: Board approval of personas is not part of the guidance; the issue is how they are written.
whyNot.3: Demographics are not a helpful basis for personas.

C.q: An agile pilot team has drafted nine personas. Why does PRINCE2 Agile advise against this many?
options: The project canvas has room for three
Too many needs blur focus and slow delivery
Each persona needs its own product owner
C.why: Too many user needs shift focus from key users, make prioritizing harder and take too long to meet deadlines (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Personas are not tied to single releases.
whyNot.1: The canvas prioritizes one to three key user groups, but that is not the persona limit or its reason.
whyNot.3: Product owners are organized by team, not by persona.

reteach.title: Cast a few characters, not a crowd
reteach.question: Why does a good novel follow a handful of characters rather than a whole city?

blocks.body: Readers care about a few well-drawn characters with clear wants. A product team is the same: a few invented people, each defined by what they need, make it easy to ask 'would this help Dev?' and to rank work. Write the cast together so builders and users' advocates share the picture, and keep it small so the story stays focused.

blocks.text: More personas is not more thorough. For pilots and new products, five is the ceiling.

explain.body: Personas help identify and articulate the specific benefits a solution can deliver to users, customers and stakeholders. They are a business case technique.

test.q: Personas mainly help the business case practice to:
test.why: They help identify and articulate the specific benefits a solution can deliver (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Story points come from relative estimation.
whyNot.1: Roles are set in the organization practice.
whyNot.2: Risk exposure is tracked with a cumulative risk burn-down chart.

explain.body: Keep personas fictional for wider innovation, and base them on user needs, not demographics.

test.q: Which persona is MOST in line with PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
options: A profile of the firm's largest real customer
A profile grouped by age, income and job title
A fictional user defined by what she needs to do
A profile copied from the board's sponsor
test.why: Personas should be fictional and built around user needs (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: Personas should be fictional, not real customers.
whyNot.1: Demographics no longer represent shared wants and needs.
whyNot.3: A real person, however senior, is not a fictional persona.

explain.body: Write personas in a cross-functional workshop that includes development team members, to increase collaboration and identification with users.

test.q: Who should be involved in writing personas, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
options: The project board, at project authorization
Project support, as the project's administrators
A single user advocate for each persona
test.why: A cross-functional workshop with development team members is highly encouraged (6.4.1).

whyNot.0: The board directs; it does not write personas.
whyNot.1: Project support handles admin and dashboards, not persona writing.
whyNot.2: One advocate writing personas loses the collaboration the workshop provides.

explain.body: No more than five for agile pilots or new products. The set can be enlarged when agile maturity is high.

items.label: maximum for pilots and new products

test.q: When can a team use more than five personas?
options: When the project is a pilot
When the product is brand new
test.why: When agile maturity is high the persona set can be enlarged; above five is not recommended for pilots or new products (6.4.1).

whyNot.1: Pilots are exactly where the limit of five applies.
whyNot.2: New products are also where the limit of five applies.
whyNot.3: The guidance links a larger set to agile maturity, not to board requests.
